tldr: By relying on a single idea—encoding traversable routes as semantic layers on a terrain mesh—this paper demonstrates that a statically unstable, two-wheeled bicycle robot can autonomously race across unstructured mountain trails at up to 18 km/h (exceeding 18 km/h and 5 m/s).
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed system. In the reinforcement learning environment TENa (B), the traversable area is provided as terrain semantics to train the policy. During real-world deployment (A), SemMap (C) builds an egocentric semantic elevation map at 30 Hz from onboard camera and LiDAR data and feeds it directly to the policy.
overview:
Mountain biking off-road takes place in brutal environments filled with steep undulations, slippery dirt, tree roots, and shifting shadows. In addition, two-wheeled bicycles are statically unstable systems that cannot stand upright at rest. Racing at high speeds without crashing requires rapid environmental perception and millisecond-level, whole-body coordinated control.

Traditional robot navigation relies on a classical control hierarchy: global planning to local planning, then to velocity commands (twist commands), and finally to limb or wheel locomotion control. However, when steering a bicycle at ultra-high speeds, this command interface becomes a bottleneck. It cannot react quickly enough to sudden wheel slips or terrain steps, leading to catastrophic failure. To solve this, the authors focused on a simple idea: directly encoding the trail to follow as a semantic layer of the terrain.

Specifically, they built a learning environment named TENa, which embeds the trail as attributes of the terrain mesh in simulation and treats local navigation and locomotion as a unified reinforcement learning (RL) problem. Without changing any reward weights, the same framework can generate both aggressive parkour and trail racing, shaped purely through terrain semantics and episode length. During real-world deployment, SemMap combines a frozen vision foundation model with a lightweight decoder to predict per-pixel terrain semantics and confidence scores from camera images. It fuses them with LiDAR point clouds to generate 30 semantic elevation maps per second on an onboard NVIDIA AGX Orin.

In field trials with the physical bicycle robot UMV, the system autonomously raced across an unstructured mountain bike trail in Zurich (roughly 1 km long) at peak speeds over 5 m/s (over 18 km/h) and an average speed of 3.26 m/s. This is 2.3 times faster than a human teleoperated baseline. In simulation, the policy also cuts failure rates by up to an order of magnitude compared to conventional hierarchical baselines.
contributions: Proposed TENa, a learning framework that unifies local navigation and locomotion into a single RL problem, eliminating intermediate velocity and pose command interfaces.
Established a design paradigm that produces both agile parkour and trail racing under fixed reward weights, guided solely by terrain mesh geometry, semantics, and episode length.

Developed SemMap, a confidence-aware semantic mapping pipeline using a frozen vision foundation model (DINOv3) and a lightweight decoder, achieving 90 Hz inference and 30 Hz map integration onboard an AGX Orin.
Demonstrated fully autonomous racing on an unstructured mountain bike trail roughly 1 km long with a two-wheeled bicycle robot, reaching peak speeds over 5 m/s and averaging 3.26 m/s.

sections.heading: Bicycle Robots Scurrying Down Trails: The Challenge of Trail Racing
sections.summary: Riding down mountain trails with a statically unstable bicycle robot requires controlling the platform at high speeds while coping with shifting friction, sunlight, and rough terrain. This work solves this problem by defining the trail as a semantic layer of the terrain and unifying navigation with locomotion.
sections.details:
Mountain bike (MTB) downhill riding demands sharp decision-making and fast reflexes even for skilled humans. Bringing this capability to robots brings severe challenges unique to outdoor forest environments. Friction changes suddenly on wet leaves and mud, tree canopies create harsh shadows, and vegetation shifts across seasons, pushing perception and control to their limits. Furthermore, unlike quadrupeds or wheeled rovers, bicycles are statically unstable systems. A slight steering delay or poor decision leads immediately to a violent crash.

Prior works have tackled autonomous car racing, drone racing, and quadruped hiking or parkour in isolation. However, none of them combined these components to push a bicycle robot to high-speed autonomy. A prior platform, the UMV (Unmanned Mountain Velocipede), featured an upper body with two active degrees of freedom and could leap 1 m vertically, but its trail runs relied entirely on human teleoperation.

Building on the UMV, this paper achieves fully autonomous trail racing through two core pillars. First, the learning framework TENa embeds the traversable path into the terrain mesh as semantic labels, solving navigation and locomotion together in a single Markov Decision Process (MDP). Second, SemMap fuses a vision foundation model and LiDAR to reconstruct an egocentric semantic elevation map onboard at 30 Hz, allowing the robot to observe the semantics in the real world. This setup enables high-speed autonomy driven purely by onboard sensing, without relying on global maps or pre-set goal coordinates.

captions.F2: Snapshots of the UMV navigating autonomously on outdoor trails and indoor parkour tracks. Using only onboard sensors, it clears tree roots, rock gardens, steep rollers, and drop-offs at speeds exceeding 18 km/h (5 m/s).

sections.heading: Limits of Control Hierarchies and the Evolution of Racing and Parkour
sections.summary: Traditional navigation relies on a hierarchy of global planning, local planning, and locomotion, but command interfaces become bottlenecks at high speeds. This work builds on end-to-end approaches from drone racing and parkour, bypassing intermediate twist commands entirely.
sections.details:
The standard pipeline for robot navigation splits the problem into three tiers: global path planning on a map, local trajectory planning for obstacle avoidance, and locomotion control to track those trajectories. However, recent breakthroughs in agile drone racing and quadruped parkour show that optimizing planning and control end-to-end through reinforcement learning offers a huge advantage when pushing systems to their dynamic limits. Conventional hierarchies rely on low-dimensional command interfaces, such as target velocity (twist) or target pose. At high speeds, these interfaces introduce information lag and discrepancies with the true terrain, triggering fatal failures.

In ground vehicle racing, mathematical optimization methods like non-linear Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) remain powerful, but they assume flat 2D tracks. In 3D drone racing, policies trained with RL directly from gate observations have outperformed human champion pilots. This work brings that philosophy into off-road wheeled robotics.

In off-road hiking, prior works have used vision-language models (VLMs) for semantic understanding or self-supervised learning for traversability estimation. However, most run at low update rates between 1 and 8 Hz, assuming slow, cautious walking. This is far too slow for a bicycle sprinting at several meters per second. This work adopts a fast feature-decoding architecture over a modern vision foundation model, achieving a rapid 90 Hz inference rate alongside accurate confidence estimation.

sections.heading: Shaping Gait via Terrains with Fixed Rewards and Real-Time Onboard Semantics
sections.summary: The proposed method consists of TENa, a procedural terrain generation environment, and SemMap, which rapidly builds semantic elevation maps from onboard camera and LiDAR data. Its key strength is unified reinforcement learning that reads the terrain directly without intermediate velocity commands.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Terrain Generation (TL and Digital Twin)
To cultivate general downhill riding skills, the authors developed the Trail Library (TL), a procedural generator producing endless trail variations. Cross-section polygons are swept along 4D paths, randomly placing skill elements such as berms, stairs, rollers, and jumps. Semantics are baked directly into the mesh vertex colors (red = trail, yellow = start, magenta = goal, blue = out-of-bounds). Over 46 km of traversable track across 1,000 terrain patches were generated. For hardware validation, high-precision Digital Twins (DT) were also scanned via LiDAR and cameras, applying geometric curricula that gradually scale track elevation.

### 3.2 Training Environment: TENa
The policy is a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Its inputs include proprioception (body tilt, angular velocities, joint angles) and a 2-layer semantic height scan (a 16x16 grid) capturing local elevation and semantics ahead. Remarkably, the policy receives neither velocity commands nor target coordinates. The reward function is simply a weighted sum of three terms:
1. Forward exploration reward $r_1$: Awarded when advancing faster than a baseline speed threshold (typically 2 m/s).
2. Course keeping reward $r_2$: A dense survival reward granted as long as a raycast beneath the chassis hits the trail mesh.
3. Trackstand reward $r_3$: A large reward granted when coming to a complete stop inside the goal zone.
Because episode lengths are fixed, reaching the goal quickly and staying parked yields a higher total return. This naturally incentivizes racing behavior—finishing in minimal time—without explicit speed targets. Reward weights remain identical across both trail racing and parkour.

### 3.3 Real-World Perception: SemMap
To run the policy on physical hardware, an egocentric 2.5D semantic elevation map matching simulation must be built in real time. The vision backbone uses DINOv3-s, a lightweight vision foundation model with frozen weights. A 320x512 image is mapped to patch features, upsampled with a lightweight upsampler (JAFAR), and fed to an ultra-compact decoder with roughly 100k parameters. The decoder has two heads: a semantic prediction head and a feature reconstruction head. Computing cosine similarity between reconstructed and original DINOv3 features provides an out-of-distribution (OOD) score, detecting novel obstacles as low confidence at zero extra runtime cost. Fusing this traversability image with LiDAR point clouds directly on the GPU updates a $15\times 15\,\text{m}^2$ local elevation map at 30 Hz.

### 3.4 Hardware and System Integration
Onboard compute consists of an UP Xtreme i12 for low-level motor control and an NVIDIA AGX Orin (64GB) dedicated to perception and state estimation. LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) provides high-frequency state estimates, while TensorRT-optimized SemMap infers at 90 Hz. To withstand crash impacts, sensors are enclosed within a rugged roll cage reinforced with Kevlar fibers and damping foam.

captions.F4: The Trail Library terrain generation pipeline. (A) Automatically sweeps cross-section polygons, merges start/goal platforms, pads margins, adds trees and rocks, and bakes vertex colors into semantics. (B) Incorporates varied skill elements like berms and rollers, using geometric height curricula (E, F) to teach complex riding behaviors.

sections.heading: From Indoor Parkour to Mountain Trails: Phased Validation and High Performance
sections.summary: After isolating Sim-to-Real control gaps on a motion-capture parkour track, the system moved to onboard indoor circuit racing (130 laps completed) and finally to a 1 km mountain trail. On natural trails, the robot averaged 3.26 m/s with peaks over 5 m/s, running 2.3 times faster than human teleoperation.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Simulation Evaluation: Parkour and Trails
Using the DT environment, the authors first trained policies across 17 extreme parkour tracks (stairs, slaloms, kickers, drop-offs). Using identical reward weights and varying only episode length, the policy reached 95% to 100% success rates on all tracks. Furthermore, on the digital twin of the Allmend Trail, tuning the maximum speed allowed the robot to hit an average speed of 9.8 m/s, matching top human rider times recorded on Strava.

### 4.2 Indoor Parkour with Motion Capture
To isolate Sim-to-Real control discrepancies, the robot ran an indoor parkour track featuring slaloms, jumps, and stair landings under a motion-capture (MoCap) system. Approaching at 3.3 m/s, taking off for 0.4 seconds of flight, landing on stairs, and transitioning to a trackstand within 0.5 seconds, the robot succeeded in 8 out of 10 runs. Failures were caused by roll tilt upon landing, exposing the hardware limit of having no roll degree of freedom in the torso.

### 4.3 Perception Pipeline (SemMap) Benchmarking
With only 20 labeled training images, SemMap achieved 33.9% mIoU on the RELLIS-3D dataset, outperforming fully fine-tuned baselines like DeepLabV3+ and SegFormer with remarkable sample efficiency. In addition, its cosine-similarity-based confidence map reliably detected unknown obstacles as OOD regions. When the camera swept away during sharp turns, low-confidence visual noise was cleanly discarded during map fusion. Complete semantic inference ran at 90 Hz (11.1 ms) on the AGX Orin.

### 4.4 Indoor Racing with Onboard Perception
Perception and control were integrated on an indoor circuit defined by white fleece fabric, featuring tight turns and slaloms. Relying strictly on onboard SemMap and LIO, the robot completed 130 consecutive laps without stopping (891 seconds total). It achieved an average speed of 3.54 m/s and reached 5 m/s on straights. The gap between simulated lap time (6.1 s) and physical lap time (6.85 s) was just 11%.

### 4.5 Autonomous Runs on the Real Allmend Trail
For the final test, the system tackled the Allmend Trail in Zurich (969 m long, 59 m elevation drop). Using a single generalist racing policy trained purely on synthetic data (TL), the robot covered the entire trail across six runs (946 m aggregate distance). The longest single continuous run was 220 m, with an average speed of 3.8 m/s and a top speed of 5.2 m/s (18.7 km/h). This was 2.3 times faster than human line-of-sight teleoperation in prior work (1.36 m/s). Advanced local path behaviors—such as charging straight over seesaws and leaning into berms on tight curves—emerged naturally from the policy without explicit heuristics.

### 4.6 Simulation Comparison with Hierarchical Baselines
Compared to classical hierarchical baselines that combine a local planner (tracking trail midlines or carrot points) with a velocity-tracking locomotion controller, the proposed method achieved substantially higher speeds. It also slashed fatal failures, like trail departures and roll-overs, by up to an order of magnitude. This clearly demonstrates the benefit of removing intermediate velocity command interfaces.

(B, C) 130-lap continuous autonomous run on an indoor circuit using only onboard sensors, along with its velocity profile. (D) Map quality comparison showing the clear benefit of confidence-aware map fusion, which filters out unreliable visual noise during sharp turns.

(B) 2.5D semantic elevation map capturing trail obstacles like seesaws and steps. (C) High traversability accuracy across varied settings—from natural trails to factory floors and city streets—using a shared frozen backbone.

sections.heading: Why It Ran Fast: Specialization, Generalization, and Bottlenecks
sections.summary: Specializing on a known course boosts top speed by 1.7x, but real-world deployment requires generalization. The authors found that the true bottleneck at high speeds was not robot dynamics, but perception look-ahead distance and resolution.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Benefits of Geometric Specialization
A specialized policy trained exclusively on the Allmend Digital Twin achieved an average speed of 5.57 m/s in simulation, roughly 1.7 times faster than the generalist policy on hardware (3.26 m/s). Specialized policies can implicitly memorize surrounding landmarks to dive aggressively into blind turns. However, because this relies on geometry and landmarks remaining unchanged across seasons, it introduces brittleness in the real world.

### 5.2 The Nature of the Sim-to-Real Gap
The main reason real-world speeds did not reach theoretical simulation limits (above 8 m/s) was not actuator saturation. Instead, it was because the MDP was deliberately tuned with safety margins to handle off-road uncertainties. In real environments with rough terrain, sensor noise, and perception latency, trading peak speed for robustness was essential.

### 5.3 Behavior at Trail Forks
When a trail branches, SemMap marks both paths as traversable. Because the policy does not receive a global destination, it naturally picks the branch that minimizes steering angle changes (the gentler curve). While this handles simple bifurcations, preventing false trail diversions in the long run will require integration with global topological maps.

### 5.4 Lessons Learned
The insights gained from this project apply broadly to agile robotics development:
- Shape behaviors through terrain meshes rather than complex rewards (a policy learns to jump simply by placing crossbars across gaps without changing reward weights).
- At high speeds, confidence weighting matters more than raw perception accuracy to prevent map corruption.
- Real-world performance was throttled by observability (missing slender obstacles or mistaking tall grass for walls) rather than dynamic limits.
- Validating across phases—from MoCap to indoor setups and then outdoors—successfully isolated and eliminated Sim-to-Real gaps one step at a time.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A Unified Architecture for Autonomous Off-Road Mobility
sections.summary: The simple concept of embedding traversable areas as terrain semantics made high-speed trail navigation possible on a demanding bicycle robot. Open-sourcing TENa and SemMap establishes a strong new baseline for autonomous trail racing.
sections.details:
This paper tackled the challenge of off-road trail racing with a statically unstable two-wheeled bicycle robot, achieving fully autonomous high-speed navigation through two key contributions: TENa and SemMap.

By dissolving the boundary between planning and control and passing trail semantics directly into the policy, the system eliminates the latency and fragility tied to intermediate velocity command interfaces. In addition, SemMap runs a frozen large-scale vision foundation model on an edge device (AGX Orin), establishing a practical perception pipeline that adapts to new environments with just a few minutes of extra data collection.

The framework also demonstrates versatility beyond bicycle robots, showing promise on quadrupeds and humanoids. The authors have open-sourced their simulation environments, perception tools, and field ROS bag datasets, providing a solid foundation to accelerate future research in agile, off-road autonomous mobility.

sections.heading: Appendix: Practical Engineering Details Behind the System
sections.summary: The appendix details PPO hyperparameters, state-action spaces, friction sampling adjustments, and cross-morphology experiments on quadrupeds and humanoids.
sections.details:
### PPO Setup and Noise Modeling
Policies are trained using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with a 3-layer MLP of 512 hidden units. Long-distance tasks like outdoor trails use larger rollout horizons than parkour tasks. To simulate real-world perception noise, three noise models are injected into the height-scan semantics during training: random label flipping (4%), dropouts of contiguous semantic blocks (20%), and distance-dependent error scaling (up to 20% on the furthest scan row).

### Improved Friction Parameter Sampling
Isaac Lab's default friction coefficient randomization clips dynamic friction to enforce the physical constraint $\mu_{\text{static}} \ge \mu_{\text{dyn}}$, which clusters samples along the diagonal where static and dynamic friction are identical. This work resolves the issue by first sampling dynamic friction uniformly, and then sampling static friction using that value as the lower bound, ensuring uniform coverage across the parameter space.

### Cross-Morphology Generalization (Quadrupeds and Humanoids)
To demonstrate the generality of the TENa framework, the quadruped robot ANYmal-D was trained using the exact same MDP and reward weights. The quadruped learned to clear difficult parkour tracks and raced through the Allmend Trail simulation at an average speed of 4.68 m/s. Furthermore, SemMap was deployed on the bipedal humanoid Unitree G1, successfully identifying and avoiding taped off-limits zones on factory floors in real time.

takeaways: Discarding intermediate velocity and pose interfaces to optimize local navigation and locomotion jointly dramatically improves robustness in extreme, agile locomotion.
Complex behaviors are far more robustly guided by designing terrain mesh geometry and semantics rather than over-engineering reward function weights.

Frozen features from large-scale pre-trained vision foundation models (like DINOv3) are expressive enough that a tiny decoder can deliver fast edge inference (90 Hz) with high sample efficiency (adapting with only 20 images).

During high-speed map fusion, rather than trusting raw visual softmax probabilities, weighting or discarding observations using objective metrics like feature reconstruction error is essential to avoid map corruption.
limitations: Tall grass or hanging twigs can be misclassified as solid obstacles and fused into the elevation map, creating 'phantom walls' that falsely block traversable trails.

Because the policy uses a coarse height scan (16x16 grid) rather than high-resolution forward imagery, slender tree roots, loose rocks, or thin poles cannot be resolved before contact and must be absorbed as unexpected physical disturbances.
Lacking global navigation goals or topological maps, the policy cannot deliberately choose between trail forks, defaulting passively to whichever branch requires the gentlest steering adjustment.
